newsitem.title: USA: Stocks end slightly higher; IBM shores up market.
newsitem.headline: Stocks end slightly higher; IBM shores up market.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks ended with small gains Wednesday as a jump in the shares of International Business Machines Corp. provided most of the luster to an otherwise dull market.

The Dow Jones industrial average ended up 1.11 points at 5,712.38. In the broader market, advancing issues beat declines 1,297 to 978 on light volume of 296 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Analysts said the rally in IBM shored up sentiment in the market, which was typically slow ahead of the Labour Day holiday weekend.
IBM gained after Salomon Brothers said the shares of the world's biggest computer maker could reach a 12-month target of $145.

"The reality is when we have a thin market like the one we have, people are likely to crowd around the one or two ideas catching the Street's attention," said Joseph Barthel, chief investment strategist at Fahnestock & Co.
John Jones, an analyst at Salomon, said he upgraded IBM to strong buy from buy, citing rising near-term confidence in the computer maker's fundamentals.
IBM, one of the 30-stock Dow Jones components, rose 2-7/8 to 114-5/8, giving a nearly nine-point lift to the index.

Other computer companies' shares also rose in sympathy, including Microsoft, which was up 7/8 to 125-5/8 and Sun MicroSystems, up 2-5/8 to 56-3/8. Alex Brown raised its 1996 and 1997 earnings estimates for Sun Micro.
Analysts said the market had entered a seasonally strong period in the three days preceding Monday's Labour Day holiday.
"Overall, approaching Labour Day historically we've had rising prices since 1896 about 80 percent of the time," said Harry Laubscher, an analyst at Tucker Anthony.

Among the big features, Philip Morris closed with a loss of 5/8 at 91-1/4 after hiking its quarterly dividend by 20 percent to $1.20 a share. The move, which had been expected, initially helped boost the stock of the world's largest cigarette maker, but it subsequently retreated.
Tobacco stocks, including Philip Morris, have suffered in recent weeks due to worries over individual and state lawsuits against the industry and increased government regulation of tobacco sales.
Philip Morris now has one of the most lucrative dividend yields among major U.S. companies.
PepsiCo lost one to 30 after Morgan Stanley trimmed its 1996 and 1997 earnings estimates for the company and lowered its expectations for the results of the Pizza Hut and Taco Bell restaurant chains.
H&R Block lost 2-1/8 to 25-3/4 and CompuServe rose 1-1/16 to 13-3/8 after H&R Block called off a proposal to spin off its 80 percent stake in the online service provider.

Analysts said the threat that 74.2 million CompuServe shares held by H&R Block could flood the market had weighed on the ailing online service firm, and Block's announcement served to mute that threat.

Among other issues, First Mississippi rose three to 27 after Mississippi Chemical, which gained 1-3/8 to 22-5/8, agreed to acquire First Mississippi's fertiliser operations in a deal valued at $297 million.
Garden Botanika slumped 4-3/4 to 8-1/2. It reported a loss for the latest quarter. The company also said its August sales were disappointing and could bode ill for its third-quarter results.
The Nasdaq Composite index rose 4.86 points to 1,153.88.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks fell 1.59 to 664.81. The American Stock Exchange index was up 1.34 to 563.39.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 0.36 to 356.79. The average share was down 4 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 6,534.140 down 1.429 or 0.02 percent.
